title: Farzi, Rishtedar, Yellow Chilli: India's Biggest Restaurant Brands Are Finally Storming America
excerpt: A Michelin-noted bistro in Bellevue, a Chilean-Indian hybrid in Miami, and Sanjeev Kapoor's chain in the Bay Area — three openings that signal a new era for Indian dining in the US.
body:
In the span of a few weeks, three of India's most prominent restaurant brands have either opened or announced their first American outposts — a convergence that suggests the long-predicted wave of Indian restaurant chains in the US is finally arriving.

Farzi Café, the Michelin Guide-recognised modern Indian bistro, has opened its doors in Bellevue, Washington, making it the brand's first US location. Rishtedar, an Indian fine-dining concept that made its name in Santiago, Chile, has debuted in Miami's Wynwood arts district. And Restaurant Business Online reports that The Yellow Chilli, fronted by celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor, is expanding its Bay Area footprint with plans for broader US growth.

The timing is not coincidental. India's restaurant industry is booming domestically, and its most ambitious operators are looking outward at a US market where Indian food remains drastically underrepresented relative to its popularity. For the Indian diaspora, these openings not only provide authentic culinary experiences but also strengthen cultural ties and offer opportunities for family gatherings and celebrations centered around Indian cuisine.

## Farzi Café: Illusion Comes to the Pacific Northwest

The name means "illusion" in Hindi, and the concept lives up to it. Farzi Café founder Zorawar Kalra — often called "the Prince of Indian Cuisine" and the son of legendary culinary figure Jiggs Kalra — has built a global network of more than two dozen restaurants across 11 countries. The London location earned recognition in the Michelin Guide. Now, the Bellevue outpost at Bellevue Square marks Kalra's most ambitious bet yet.

The menu features dishes designed to challenge what Americans think Indian food can be: Dal Chawal Arancini, Paneer Lasagna, Achari Chicken Tacos, and a Parle-G Cheesecake that turns India's most iconic biscuit into a dessert. The cocktail programme includes astrology-inspired "Farzified" drinks that lean into theatrical presentation.

"Making Indian cuisine a mainstream cuisine across the US" is Kalra's stated mission, and he is planning locations coast to coast. This expansion not only enhances the culinary landscape for NRIs but also creates potential job opportunities for Indian chefs and hospitality professionals in the US.

## Rishtedar: From Santiago to Wynwood

Rishtedar's path to America is perhaps the most unexpected of the three. Founded by Vikram Thadani, who was born to Indian parents in Chile, the brand started as an import business before evolving into a fine-dining restaurant in Santiago. The name means "family" in Hindi.

The Wynwood location, designed by Mico Design & Co. with interiors full of bright colours and textures reflecting Indian culture, serves a menu that blends South American sensibility with Indian tradition. Think tandoor-cooked chicken with tikka sauce served with blazing charcoal underneath, sesame-breaded shrimp with 12 spices, and butter chicken alongside lamb in onion-masala sauce.

"Creating an experience that captures my heritage and can serve as an introduction to Indian culture was our aim," Thadani says. For Miami's diverse dining scene, the addition of a Latin American-inflected Indian restaurant feels both novel and inevitable. For NRIs in Miami, Rishtedar offers a unique dining experience that bridges their cultural heritage with local culinary trends.

## The Yellow Chilli: Sanjeev Kapoor's Quiet Expansion

While Farzi and Rishtedar generate headlines with their openings, Sanjeev Kapoor's The Yellow Chilli has been quietly building its American presence from the Bay Area. The chain already operates in Santa Clara and Danville, positioning itself as a family-friendly casual dining option with moderate prices — a counterpoint to the fine-dining approach of the other two.

The menu reads like a "gastronomic tour of India," featuring Kapoor's signature dishes: Lalla Mussa Dal (black and green lentils slow-cooked overnight with cream, ghee, and butter), Shaam Savera (spinach koftas in tomato butter gravy), and Puran Singh da Tariwala Murgh (chicken curry inspired by roadside dhabas on the Ambala-Delhi highway).

With about 30 locations in India and branches in the UAE and Oman, The Yellow Chilli's American strategy is methodical: establish a beachhead in Silicon Valley's Indian American heartland, then expand outward. This approach not only caters to the tastes of the Indian diaspora but also helps introduce Indian flavors to a broader audience.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs who have long lamented that America's Indian restaurant scene is stuck in a rut of identikit tikka masala joints, this is a moment to pay attention. The arrival of brands like Farzi, Rishtedar, and The Yellow Chilli represents something new: Indian restaurateurs who have already proven their concepts in competitive international markets now bringing that sophistication to the United States.

The implications extend beyond the dining table. Each successful Indian restaurant chain normalises Indian cuisine for mainstream American audiences, moves the conversation beyond "spicy or mild," and creates career pathways for Indian chefs and hospitality professionals in the US. Additionally, these restaurants foster community among NRIs, providing spaces for cultural exchange and connection.

## What's Next

The pipeline shows no signs of slowing. The Kati Roll Company continues to expand its grab-and-go Indian street food concept across New York City, now at six locations. Industry data from Technomic shows that 34 percent of American consumers who have tried Indian food consider it "unique and exciting" — a massive untapped market. The question for India's restaurant chains is no longer whether America is ready. It is how fast they can build.
